questions.stem: The strike of a tilted rock layer is:
options: the angle between the surface of the layer and a horizontal plane
the thickness of the layer measured at right angles to its surface
the direction in which water would flow straight down the layer
the compass direction of a horizontal line on the surface of the layer
questions.explanation: Strike is the trend of a horizontal line drawn on a bedding plane. The angle of tilt is the dip, and the direction water would run down the surface is the dip direction.

questions.stem: The dip of a rock layer is recorded as:
options: the angle of the layer below horizontal and its direction, measured at right angles to strike
the compass bearing of a horizontal line drawn on the layer, measured parallel to its strike direction
the distance from the layer to the nearest outcrop of the same rock type
the depth below the surface at which the layer was first found by drilling
questions.explanation: Dip is the steepest angle between the bedding plane and the horizontal, together with the direction it slopes down. It is always perpendicular to strike.

questions.stem: A sandstone bed strikes north-south. In which directions could it dip?
options: North-east or south-west
Straight down only
East or west
North or south
questions.explanation: Dip direction is at right angles to strike. A bed striking north-south can only dip towards the east or towards the west.

questions.stem: Why are geological cross-sections drawn along a line perpendicular to the strike of the beds?
options: The section then shows the beds as horizontal, which makes the drawing simpler to read
The section then avoids crossing any faults, which cannot be shown on cross-sections
The section then shows the strike as a steeper angle than the true dip of the beds
The section then shows the true dip, while an oblique line shows a smaller apparent dip
questions.explanation: Only a section at right angles to strike cuts the beds along their steepest slope. Any other section line shows an apparent dip that is less than the true dip.

questions.stem: On a geological map, how do the contacts between horizontal beds appear?
options: They form circles centred on the highest hilltop
They run at right angles across the contour lines
They follow the contour lines, staying at the same height
They form straight lines that ignore the topography
questions.explanation: A horizontal contact is at one elevation everywhere, so it runs parallel to the contours. Steeper beds cut increasingly across them.

questions.stem: Contacts between some beds cross hills and valleys on a map as perfectly straight lines. What does this show?
options: The beds are horizontal, so their outcrop follows the topography
The beds dip gently, so they form wide V shapes in each valley
The beds are folded, so they repeat on both sides of each hill
The beds are vertical, so their outcrop is not affected by topography
questions.explanation: A vertical plane intersects any land surface along a straight line in map view. The more gently a bed dips, the more its outcrop is bent by valleys and ridges.

questions.stem: Where a stream valley crosses the outcrop of a tilted bed, the contact forms a V on the map pointing downstream. What does this show about the bed?
options: It dips downstream, more steeply than the valley floor slopes
It dips upstream, into the hillside at the head of the valley
It is horizontal, lying at the same height along the valley
It is vertical, so the valley has no effect on its outcrop
questions.explanation: By the rule of Vs, beds dipping downstream more steeply than the stream gradient V downstream. Horizontal beds and beds dipping upstream V upstream, and vertical beds do not V at all.

questions.stem: On a geological map, how can an eroded anticline be recognised?
options: The beds are not repeated, and all of them dip in the same direction across the map
The beds form straight lines that cut across the contours at right angles everywhere
The oldest beds are in the centre, repeated in order on both sides, dipping away from the axis
The youngest beds are in the centre, repeated in order on both sides, dipping towards the axis
questions.explanation: An anticline is an upfold, so erosion of its crest exposes the oldest rocks along the axis. Beds dip away from the axis on either limb. A syncline shows the opposite pattern.

questions.stem: Across a map, beds outcrop in the order D, C, B, C, D, where D is the oldest bed. The dips on both sides point towards B. Which structure is this?
options: An anticline
A normal fault
A dyke
A syncline
questions.explanation: The youngest bed, B, lies in the centre, and the limbs dip towards it, so the structure is a downfold, or syncline.

questions.stem: In a cross-section, beds are repeated symmetrically about a central bed, and the central bed is the oldest. The two limbs dip away from the centre at 40° and 20°. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a syncline, and it is symmetrical because the oldest bed is in the centre
It is an anticline, and it is asymmetrical because the limbs dip at different angles
It is a syncline, and it is asymmetrical because the limbs dip at different angles
It is an anticline, and it is symmetrical because the beds repeat on both sides
questions.explanation: Oldest rocks in the core with limbs dipping away identify an anticline. Limbs with different dips make the fold asymmetrical, even though the beds repeat on both sides.

questions.stem: On a cross-section, the block above a dipping fault plane (the hanging wall) has moved down relative to the block below. Which description is correct?
options: A normal fault, caused by tension pulling the crust apart
A reverse fault, caused by compression pushing the crust together
A strike-slip fault, caused by blocks sliding horizontally past each other
An unconformity, caused by erosion of the hanging wall before deposition
questions.explanation: In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down, lengthening the crust, which happens under tension. In a reverse fault the hanging wall moves up under compression.

questions.stem: Which type of fault forms when compression pushes the hanging wall up relative to the footwall?
options: A conformable fault
A reverse fault
A normal fault
A strike-slip fault
questions.explanation: Compression shortens the crust by pushing the hanging wall up and over the footwall. A low-angle reverse fault is called a thrust fault.

questions.stem: A fault cuts a sequence of tilted beds, and the land surface has since been eroded flat. On the map, older beds are exposed on the east side of the fault. Which side was upthrown?
options: Both sides equally, because erosion removes the same rock from each
The east side, because uplift and erosion expose older, deeper beds
The west side, because the downthrown side always exposes older beds
Neither side, because faults never change the beds exposed at the surface
questions.explanation: Erosion planes off the upthrown block more deeply into the sequence, exposing older rocks. So, after erosion, older beds at the surface mark the upthrown side.

questions.stem: On a geological map, the contacts of a set of folded beds end abruptly against the base of a flat-lying sandstone that covers them. What does this show?
options: A normal fault: the sandstone has dropped down against the folded beds beside it
An angular unconformity: the beds were folded and eroded before the sandstone was deposited
A conformable sequence: the sandstone was deposited first and the older beds were folded much later
A dyke: the sandstone was injected as magma that cut through the folded beds
questions.explanation: The folded beds must have been deformed and eroded before the younger, flat sandstone was laid across their truncated edges. The sandstone is younger than both the beds and the folding.

questions.stem: What does a stratigraphic column show?
options: The sequence of rock units at a location, oldest at the base, with thicknesses and rock types
The map view of rock units across a whole region, with strike and dip symbols drawn for each bed
The positions of the continents through time, with the oldest at the top of the page
The chemical composition of each mineral in a rock, from the most to least abundant
questions.explanation: A stratigraphic column is a vertical summary of the rock layers at one place, drawn to scale, with symbols for rock types and often fossils and sedimentary structures.

questions.stem: A stratigraphic column is drawn at a scale of 1 cm to 5 m. A shale unit on it is 3.2 cm tall. How thick is the shale?
questions.explanation: Thickness = 3.2 × 5 = 16 m. Adding 5 to 3.2, or using the wrong scale factor, gives the other values.

questions.stem: The same distinctive sandstone appears in two stratigraphic columns 10 km apart. It is 20 m thick in column A and 5 m thick in column B. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: The sandstone at A must have been folded, which always doubles a unit's thickness
The unit thins from A towards B, so more sand was deposited, or less eroded, near A
The units cannot be the same, because a rock unit always has the same thickness
The sandstone at B is older, because thinner units are always older than thick ones
questions.explanation: Units can be correlated by their distinctive features even if their thickness changes. Thinning usually reflects less sediment supply or erosion of the top of the unit towards one site.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of a block diagram over a geological map alone?
options: It shows the map view and cross-sections together, so the 3D shape of structures is clear
It shows the exact age of every rock unit in millions of years, written beside each of the layers
It shows only the surface of the land, without any information about depth
It replaces the need for field data, because it is drawn without any measurements
questions.explanation: A block diagram shows the top surface and two or more sides of a block of crust, helping to visualise how beds, folds, faults and intrusions extend underground.

questions.stem: A tilted bed outcrops on flat ground with a width of 20 m measured perpendicular to strike. The bed dips at 30°. What is its true thickness?
questions.explanation: On flat ground, true thickness = outcrop width × sin(dip) = 20 × sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m. Using cos 30° gives about 17 m.

questions.stem: Why does a geologist record a GPS position for every observation and sample in the field?
options: So each observation can be located accurately on a map and revisited later
So the age of each sample can be calculated from its position on Earth
So the rock type of each sample can be identified without examining it
So the strike and dip of every bed can be measured without a compass
questions.explanation: Map and field location techniques let data be plotted and checked. Without accurate locations, observations cannot be built into a map or cross-section.

questions.stem: A student measures the strike of a bed with a compass while holding a steel rock hammer beside it. What kind of error is likely?
options: A random error, because the steel makes the needle swing in a different direction each time
No error, because compasses are not affected by nearby iron or steel objects
A parallax error, because the hammer blocks the student's view of the clinometer scale
A systematic error, because the steel deflects the compass needle the same way each time
questions.explanation: Steel tools, vehicles and magnetite-rich rocks distort the magnetic field near the compass, shifting readings consistently. Moving the hammer away removes the error.

questions.stem: Why should a photograph of an outcrop include an object of known size, such as a hammer or scale bar, and a note of the direction faced?
options: So the age of the rocks can be read directly from the size of the object shown
So the camera can focus properly, since outcrops have no detail of their own
So the size and orientation of features can be judged when the photo is interpreted later
So that the photograph can be used instead of collecting any field measurements at the outcrop
questions.explanation: Without a scale and orientation, a photograph cannot show whether a feature is centimetres or metres across, or which way beds dip. Good field records support later analysis.

questions.stem: Why should rock samples for identification be broken to show a fresh surface?
options: Fresh surfaces are always harder, which makes the rock easier to carry home
Weathered surfaces are radioactive, so they must be removed for safety
Fresh surfaces show the age of the rock, which weathered surfaces cannot
Weathered surfaces can change colour and texture, leading to misidentification
questions.explanation: Weathering stains and softens rock surfaces and alters minerals. Identifying rocks from weathered surfaces is a common source of error, which a fresh surface avoids.

questions.stem: Which precaution should be part of a risk assessment for collecting rock samples with a hammer?
options: Wearing safety glasses, because flying rock chips can injure eyes
Hammering the rock next to a classmate so they can see the result
Working directly beneath an overhanging cliff for shade
Leaving the first aid kit in the vehicle to reduce weight
questions.explanation: Hammering can send sharp chips flying, so eye protection is essential. Other risks include falling rock near cliffs, heat and remote locations.

questions.stem: A class plans to collect rock and soil samples on a farm and in a nearby national park. Which action is required for ethical fieldwork?
options: Avoiding any record of sample locations, so others cannot find the same sites
Getting permission from the landholder and checking park rules before collecting anything
Collecting as many samples as possible, since rocks are a renewable resource
Removing fossils from the national park, since they are of no scientific value if left in place
questions.explanation: Research ethics include respecting land access rights, protected areas and heritage, and minimising disturbance. National parks generally prohibit collecting without a permit.

questions.stem: Students compare the salinity of water at five sites along a creek. Which procedure would give the most valid and reliable comparison?
options: Sample at the same depth and time of day at each site, and repeat at each site
Sample at whatever depth is easiest at each site, and take a single sample each
Sample each site on a different day, starting upstream after the heaviest rain
Sample only the site with the clearest water, and assume the others are the same
questions.explanation: Controlling depth and time removes variables that could change salinity, and repeated samples show the variation at each site. Environmental sampling must be methodical to produce valid data.

questions.stem: Five students measure the dip of the same bedding surface: 28°, 31°, 30°, 45° and 29°. What is the best interpretation?
options: The data show no pattern, so the dip of the bed cannot be estimated at all
The 45° reading is probably an error, such as a measurement on a joint, and should be checked
The 45° reading must be correct, because the largest value measured is always the most accurate one
The bed must dip at 45°, because one careful reading outweighs the four others
questions.explanation: Four readings agree within a few degrees, but one is far from the rest. It may come from measuring a joint or an uneven surface, so it should be rechecked rather than averaged in.

questions.stem: Foliation in a metamorphic rock is:
options: a set of curved, shell-like surfaces formed when the rock is broken
a parallel alignment of platy minerals or banding produced by directed pressure
a set of rounded holes left by gas bubbles in rock that cooled from lava
a series of layers of different sediments laid down in water over time
questions.explanation: Under directed pressure, platy minerals such as mica grow or rotate perpendicular to the greatest stress, giving the rock a planar fabric or banding.

questions.stem: As a shale is subjected to increasing metamorphic grade, which sequence of rocks forms?
options: Gneiss, schist, phyllite, slate
Schist, slate, gneiss, phyllite
Phyllite, gneiss, slate, schist
Slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss
questions.explanation: With rising temperature and pressure, mica crystals grow larger and minerals segregate: slate, then phyllite, then schist with visible mica, then banded gneiss.

questions.stem: A fine-grained, dark grey rock splits into thin, flat, smooth sheets, but individual minerals cannot be seen. Which rock is it?
options: Slate
Schist
Gneiss
Marble
questions.explanation: Slate is low-grade metamorphosed shale or mudstone. Its microscopic aligned micas give slaty cleavage, which is why it is used for roofing tiles.

questions.stem: A fine-grained foliated rock has a silky sheen and slightly wavy cleavage surfaces, but its mica crystals are too small to see. Which rock is it?
options: Schist
Quartzite
Phyllite
Slate
questions.explanation: Phyllite is between slate and schist in grade. Its mica is coarser than in slate, enough to give a sheen, but finer than the visible flakes in schist.

questions.stem: A rock contains many visible, parallel flakes of mica that make its surface sparkle. Which rock is it?
options: Schist
Slate
Marble
Amphibolite
questions.explanation: Schist is a medium- to high-grade foliated rock in which mica crystals are large enough to see. Their alignment gives the foliation called schistosity.

questions.stem: A coarse-grained rock shows alternating light bands of quartz and feldspar and dark bands of biotite and hornblende. Which rock is it?
options: Granite
Schist
Phyllite
Gneiss
questions.explanation: Gneissic banding forms at high metamorphic grade when light and dark minerals separate into layers. Granite has a similar composition but its crystals are randomly arranged, not banded.

questions.stem: Which metamorphic rock is matched with its correct protolith?
options: Marble from dolerite
Marble from limestone
Quartzite from basalt
Amphibolite from sandstone
questions.explanation: Marble forms from limestone, quartzite from sandstone, and amphibolite from mafic igneous rocks such as basalt and dolerite.

questions.stem: Two pale, non-foliated metamorphic rocks look alike. One fizzes in dilute hydrochloric acid and is scratched by a steel nail; the other does not fizz and scratches glass. Which are they?
options: Both are marble, formed from different limestones
The first is marble and the second is quartzite
The first is quartzite and the second is marble
The first is slate and the second is gneiss
questions.explanation: Marble is recrystallised calcite: hardness 3 and reactive with acid. Quartzite is recrystallised quartz: hardness 7 and unreactive.

questions.stem: A dark, medium- to coarse-grained metamorphic rock is made mainly of hornblende and plagioclase. Which rock is it, and what was its protolith?
options: Amphibolite, from basalt or dolerite
Quartzite, from sandstone
Marble, from limestone
Slate, from shale
questions.explanation: Metamorphism of mafic igneous rock converts pyroxene and plagioclase to hornblende and plagioclase, forming amphibolite.

questions.stem: Sandstone breaks around its sand grains, but quartzite formed from it breaks straight through the grains. Why?
options: Weathering removed the cement from quartzite, leaving loose grains that break when struck
Recrystallisation fused the quartz into an interlocking mosaic stronger than the grains themselves
Metamorphism softened the quartz grains so much that they now break more easily than the cement
Quartzite contains no quartz, so its grains are weaker than those of the original sandstone
questions.explanation: During metamorphism quartz grains recrystallise and grow into each other, so the boundaries are no longer weak cement. A fracture then passes through the grains.

questions.stem: Marble and quartzite usually show no foliation, even when they formed under directed pressure. Why?
options: They form only by contact metamorphism beside intrusions, which never involves any directed pressure at all
They are igneous rocks, so they crystallised from magma and were never metamorphosed
Their foliation is always removed by weathering soon after they reach the surface
They are made mostly of calcite or quartz, which form equidimensional grains rather than platy minerals
questions.explanation: Foliation needs platy or elongated minerals that can align. Calcite and quartz crystals are roughly equidimensional, so these rocks stay massive even under directed stress.
